526.title: Vayelech: the hidden face (Deuteronomy 31:17–18)
526.hook: the Torah foresees times when God's face seems hidden
526.howItsDone: Hester panim is a central idea in Jewish reflection on suffering and divine silence, and the book of Esther, read on Purim, is often taught as its great example: a story in which God is never named.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last commandment: write this song. Your line was write your own. What did you copy by hand? Today, a hard verse from the same chapter. Day five hundred twenty-six.

There's a silence that comes after you pray, or hope, or ask, and nothing answers. People of faith have written about it for thousands of years. The Psalms are full of it: a voice asking how long God will hide His face. It can feel like the opposite of everything religion promises. What's surprising is that the Torah itself sees this silence coming. Before the people even cross the river, God tells Moses there will be times like this.
screen: `AFTER THE ASKING, SILENCE.` → `HOW LONG WILT THOU HIDE?` → `THE TORAH SEES IT COMING.`

segments.voice: God tells Moses that in time the people will stray, and troubles will find them. Then: "And I will surely hide My face in that day." In Hebrew, haster astir panai. From it comes a phrase Jewish thought has carried for centuries: hester panim, the hiding of the face. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say God leaves, or stops existing, or stops caring. A face that's hidden is still there. And the verse lets the people speak their pain: are not these evils come upon us, they ask, because our God is not among us? The text puts that feeling into words. It doesn't pretend the silence is easy. The rabbis found a quiet surprise inside the Hebrew. The Talmud, in Chullin, asks where the book of Esther is hinted at in the Torah, and answers with this verse: haster astir, I will surely hide. Esther. It's the one book of the Bible in which God is never named, and yet its story turns, again and again, at just the right moment. Hidden, the rabbis suggest, isn't the same as absent. After the Holocaust, some Jewish thinkers reached for hester panim to name what had happened. Others found even that phrase too small, or refused any explanation at all. Both responses live inside the tradition. What the verse offers is permission to name the silence honestly, without calling it the end.
screen: `HASTER ASTIR: I WILL HIDE.` · `A HIDDEN FACE IS STILL THERE.` · `ESTHER: GOD NEVER NAMED.` · `NAMING THE SILENCE HONESTLY.` · then, large: `HIDDEN, NOT GONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit honestly with silence. Settle, and breathe. Don't fill the quiet. If there's something you've asked for or hoped for that hasn't come, let it be there. You don't have to explain it, and you don't have to defend anyone. If you pray, you can bring the psalm's old question, how long, and let it stand without an answer. If you don't, simply sit with the quiet as it is, and notice that you're still here inside it. The bell holds the time.
Hester panim. The hiding of the face. A silence the Torah foresaw, and called hidden, not gone.
Your line: hidden, not gone. Today, if something feels absent, try the word hidden instead, and see whether it changes anything. Day five hundred twenty-six.

screen: `DAY 526 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HA'AZINU: GIVE EAR, O HEAVENS (DEUTERONOMY 32:1).`

527.title: Ha'azinu: give ear, O heavens (Deuteronomy 32:1)
527.hook: Moses' last song calls heaven and earth as witnesses
527.howItsDone: Ha'azinu is read in synagogue in the fall, usually on the Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur or just after; in the Torah scroll it is written in a special two-column layout.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hester panim, the hidden face. Your line was hidden, not gone. Did the word hidden change anything? Today, Moses stops speaking and starts to sing. Day five hundred twenty-seven.

Open a Torah scroll almost anywhere and you see columns of text running edge to edge, like the pages of a book. Then you reach Ha'azinu, and the page changes shape. The words split into two narrow columns with a gap down the middle, line answering line. Scribes still copy it that way today. Even someone who can't read a word of Hebrew can see that something different is happening. Moses' last long words aren't a speech. They're a song.
screen: `COLUMNS, EDGE TO EDGE.` → `THEN, A PAGE IN TWO.` → `NOT A SPEECH: A SONG.`

segments.voice: It begins: "Give ear, ye heavens, and I will speak; And let the earth hear the words of my mouth." Ha'azinu means give ear: listen closely. In Nitzavim, Moses had called heaven and earth as witnesses. Now he speaks to them directly. Why the sky and the ground? Rashi gives two reasons. First, they last. Moses is mortal, and so is everyone listening, but heaven and earth will still be there to testify long after. Second, they respond. If the people keep the covenant, the heavens give rain and the earth gives its crops; if not, they hold back. Witnesses that can act. There's a playful midrash in the Sifrei too. Moses says give ear to the heavens, the word for listening up close, and only hear to the earth, the word for listening from further off, because he was near to heaven and far from earth. The prophet Isaiah, the midrash notes, says it the other way round: hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth. He was nearer the earth. Under the play is a real point: where you stand shapes how you speak. The song itself is long and fierce, a retelling of the people's whole history, its gifts and its failures. It's read in synagogue in the fall, around the High Holy Days. And it opens by calling the whole world to listen: the sky above, the ground below, and everyone in between.
screen: `HA'AZINU: GIVE EAR.` · `WITNESSES THAT LAST.` · `WITNESSES THAT RESPOND.` · `ISAIAH SAYS IT THE OTHER WAY.` · then, large: `HEAVEN AND EARTH LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at sky and earth. If you can, go to a window or step outside. If not, picture them. Look up first: the sky, whatever it's doing right now, cloud or blue or dark. Then look down: the ground, the floor, grass, pavement. Moses called these two to listen because they last. Let yourself be small between them for a moment. Breathe in the space between above and below. The bell holds the time.
Ha'azinu. Give ear. The first word of Moses' last song, spoken to the sky.
Your line: heaven and earth listen. Today, look up once and down once, on purpose, and remember who Moses called to listen. Day five hundred twenty-seven.

528.title: Ha'azinu: like rain (Deuteronomy 32:2)
528.hook: "My doctrine shall drop as the rain", softly and over time
528.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often cite this verse, and the rabbinic comparison of Torah to water, to describe patient, gradual learning, such as the weekly cycle of Torah reading and daily study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the song began: give ear, ye heavens. Your line was heaven and earth listen. Did you look up, and down? Today, the very next verse, and the weather. Day five hundred twenty-eight.

A cloudburst and a long drizzle can drop the same amount of water. But after a cloudburst, much of it runs off. The ground is hard, the water comes too fast, and it rushes into the gutters. After a slow, soft rain, the soil drinks most of it in. Any gardener can tell you this. Moses, beginning his last song, says that's exactly how he wants his teaching to arrive.
screen: `A CLOUDBURST RUNS OFF.` → `A SOFT RAIN SOAKS IN.` → `HOW TEACHING SHOULD ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: "My doctrine shall drop as the rain, My speech shall distil as the dew; As the small rain upon the tender grass, And as the showers upon the herb." Four pictures of water, each one gentle. Rain. Dew. Small rain on tender grass. Showers on the herb. The Hebrew word behind doctrine is likchi, my teaching, from a root that means to take, to receive. Teaching is something received. Notice the pace of the verse. Rain doesn't fall all at once. Dew arrives overnight, drop by drop, and nobody sees it come. Tender grass can't take a flood. Moses is describing how teaching lands: slowly, in amounts a listener can hold, over time. The rabbis loved comparing Torah to water. The Talmud, in Taanit, says: just as water flows down from a high place to a low one, Torah settles in a person who is humble. And the Sifrei gives another picture. The same rain falls on the whole field, and each plant grows in its own way: the vine one way, the olive another, the fig another. The same teaching, falling on different people, helps each one grow into who they are. Good teachers seem to know this without being told. They don't pour everything out in one class. They come back week after week, a little at a time, and wait for it to soak in.
screen: `RAIN, DEW, SMALL RAIN, SHOWERS.` · `LIKCHI: TEACHING, RECEIVED.` · `WATER SEEKS THE LOW PLACE.` · `ONE RAIN, EACH PLANT ITS OWN WAY.` · then, large: `DROP AS THE RAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: teach gently, not all at once. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you're trying to teach, or help, or change. A child, a new coworker, a partner, maybe yourself. Have you been pouring it on? Picture a slow rain instead. What's the smallest piece you could offer today? One sentence, one example, one patient answer. Then picture leaving the rest for another day, and trusting it to soak in. The bell holds the time.
Ha'azinu. Give ear. And the song's second verse: teaching that falls like rain and settles like dew.
Your line: drop as the rain. Today, when you explain something, give one small piece, and stop there. Day five hundred twenty-eight.

529.title: Ha'azinu: the Rock (Deuteronomy 32:4)
529.hook: God is called "The Rock, His work is perfect"
529.howItsDone: The phrase 'the Rock, His work is perfect' opens tzidduk hadin, recited at Jewish burials, and many Jews close the Amidah with Psalm 19:15, 'my Rock, and my Redeemer'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, teaching that drops like rain. Your line was drop as the rain. Did you offer one small piece? Today, a name for God that you could almost hold in your hand. Day five hundred twenty-nine.

Rain soaks in and moves on. Two verses later, the song reaches for the opposite picture: something that doesn't move at all. A great boulder at the edge of a field, or in the middle of a riverbed. The water goes around it for centuries. People sit on it, lean against it, give directions by it: turn left at the big rock. In Ha'azinu, Moses takes that rock and makes it a name.
screen: `A BOULDER IN THE RIVERBED.` → `TURN LEFT AT THE BIG ROCK.` → `A ROCK BECOMES A NAME.`

segments.voice: "The Rock, His work is perfect; For all His ways are justice." The Hebrew is tzur: rock, the solid kind, a cliff face or a boulder. Ha'azinu comes back to the word for God several times. A rock is what you build on, what you shelter behind, what's still there when everything else washes away. In the wilderness, rock meant shade and refuge, and twice in the story, even water. Then the song turns the image around. When the people grow comfortable, it says, they scorned the Rock of their salvation. You can lean on a rock, and you can also forget it's there at all. The picture went deep into Jewish prayer. At the end of the Amidah, the standing prayer, many people say a verse from the Psalms: "Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before Thee, O LORD, my Rock, and my Redeemer." And this very verse, the Rock, His work is perfect, opens the prayer called tzidduk hadin, accepting the judgment, said at Jewish funerals, when a family is at its least steady. In that moment it can be a very hard sentence to say. That may be part of its point. The Rock doesn't promise that everything will feel right. It names something that stays when nothing else does.
screen: `TZUR: THE ROCK.` · `SHELTER, SHADE, WATER.` · `A ROCK YOU CAN FORGET.` · `MY ROCK, AND MY REDEEMER.` · then, large: `THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a stone and steady yourself. If there's a stone nearby, pick it up. If not, a mug, a book, anything solid. Feel the weight in your palm. Notice that it doesn't change while you breathe. Your thoughts move, your mood moves, the day moves. The stone just sits there. If you pray, you can say the psalm's old words: my Rock, and my Redeemer. If not, simply let your hand rest on something that stays. The bell holds the time.
Ha'azinu. Give ear. And tzur: the Rock, the name the song gives God again and again.
Your line: the rock. Today, when something shakes you, put your hand on something solid for one breath. Day five hundred twenty-nine.

530.title: Ha'azinu: ask your father (Deuteronomy 32:7)
530.hook: remember the days of old; ask your father and your elders
530.tomorrow: Ha'azinu: the eagle over its nest (Deuteronomy 32:11)
530.howItsDone: Jewish learning is built on chains of transmission, from teacher to student and parent to child; Pirkei Avot opens with that chain, and the Passover seder is structured around children's questions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzur, the Rock. Your line was the rock. What did you put your hand on? Today, the song tells you where to go for answers. Day five hundred thirty.

After someone dies, a particular kind of regret often arrives. Not about what you said to them. About what you never asked. How did you two meet? What was your own grandfather like? What was the hardest year of your life? The answers went with them. Almost anyone who has lost a grandparent knows the feeling. In the middle of Ha'azinu, between the Rock and the history of the people, Moses' song gives an instruction that would have prevented it.
screen: `AFTER THE FUNERAL.` → `THE QUESTIONS NEVER ASKED.` → `THE SONG'S INSTRUCTION.`

segments.voice: "Remember the days of old, Consider the years of many generations; Ask thy father, and he will declare unto thee, Thine elders, and they will tell thee." Two pairs. Remember and consider: work you do inside your own head. Ask and be told: work that needs another person. The verse doesn't trust memory alone. You have to go and ask. Father and elders form a kind of ladder. Your father knows his own years. The elders reach further back. And Jewish tradition is built like that ladder. The tractate Pirkei Avot opens with a chain: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly. Each link asked, and was told. The Passover seder runs on asking too. The night is shaped around a child's questions. Notice where the verse puts the responsibility. On the younger one. Ask. The elders' part is to declare and to tell, but they can only answer what someone thinks to ask. Many old people carry stories no one has ever asked for. Many families have one person who knows where everyone came from, and only a few years left to say it. The song puts it plainly: memory isn't only kept. It has to be asked for.
screen: `REMEMBER, CONSIDER, ASK.` · `A LADDER OF GENERATIONS.` · `MOSES TO JOSHUA TO THE ELDERS.` · `THE YOUNGER ONE ASKS.` · then, large: `ASK YOUR ELDERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask an elder one question. Settle, and breathe. Think of the oldest person you could reach this week. A parent, a grandparent, an old neighbor, a former teacher, someone at your congregation. What don't you know about their life? Choose one question. Not a quiz; a door. What was your first job? Who taught you to cook? What do you remember about your own grandparents? Hold that question until you can ask it. The bell holds the time.
Ha'azinu. Give ear. And in it, a command to ask: ask thy father, thine elders.
Your line: ask your elders. Today, or this week, ask one older person one question about their life, and listen to the whole answer. Day five hundred thirty.

531.title: Ha'azinu: the eagle over its nest (Deuteronomy 32:11)
531.hook: God cares like an eagle that stirs its nest and spreads its wings
531.tomorrow: V'Zot HaBerachah: end with a blessing (Deuteronomy 33:1)
531.howItsDone: The image of God bearing Israel on eagles' wings, from Exodus 19 and Ha'azinu, is a familiar one in Jewish teaching and song, often used to describe care that protects without smothering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a command to ask your father and your elders. Your line was ask your elders. What question are you holding? Today, a bird. Day five hundred thirty-one.

Sooner or later, a young bird has to leave the nest. It doesn't want to. The nest is warm, food arrives on schedule, and the edge looks very far down. The parent bird has a problem: how do you push someone toward the thing that scares them without letting them fall? Parents of teenagers know this problem well. So do teachers, coaches, anyone who has ever helped another person grow up. Ha'azinu answers it with a picture.
screen: `A WARM NEST, A LONG DROP.` → `PUSH, BUT DON'T LET THEM FALL.` → `THE SONG'S PICTURE.`

segments.voice: "As an eagle that stirreth up her nest, Hovereth over her young, Spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, Beareth them on her pinions." That's how, the song says, God cared for the people in the wilderness. Four movements. Stir the nest: wake them, get them ready. Hover: stay close, without pressing down. Spread the wings: make a place for them to land. Bear them up: carry them while they can't yet fly. Rashi reads the details tenderly. The eagle, he says, doesn't swoop straight down onto its young. It flutters over the nest to wake them gently, and hovers without putting its full weight on them. And when it carries them, it carries them on its wings, not in its claws. Other birds, Rashi says, carry their young in their feet, because they fear a bigger bird above. The eagle fears only an arrow shot from below, so it puts its own body between the arrow and its young. The same picture appears at Sinai, in Exodus, where God says to the people: "how I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself." Protection here isn't keeping someone in the nest forever. It's stirring them to grow, and staying underneath while they learn to fly.
screen: `STIR, HOVER, SPREAD, BEAR.` · `NO FULL WEIGHT ON THE NEST.` · `ON THE WINGS, NOT IN THE CLAWS.` · `I BORE YOU ON EAGLES' WINGS.` · then, large: `SPREAD THE WINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: protect someone gently. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you care for who's trying something new. Where are you on the eagle's list? Stirring them, hovering, spreading your wings, carrying them? Maybe you've been pressing down with your full weight, or holding on too tightly. Picture loosening your grip. Staying close, staying underneath, letting them try. And if you are the one in the nest right now, picture someone hovering nearby, close enough to catch you if you fall. The bell holds the time.
Ha'azinu. Give ear. And the eagle in the song, stirring the nest and spreading its wings beneath its young.
Your line: spread the wings. Today, protect someone by staying close and letting them try, not by doing it for them. Day five hundred thirty-one.

screen: `DAY 531 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: V'ZOT HABERACHAH: END WITH A BLESSING (DEUTERONOMY 33:1).`

532.title: V'Zot HaBerachah: end with a blessing (Deuteronomy 33:1)
532.hook: Moses' last act is to bless each tribe
532.howItsDone: V'Zot HaBerachah is read on Simchat Torah rather than on a Shabbat. On Friday nights many Jewish parents bless their children with the priestly blessing from Numbers 6.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eagle that spreads its wings beneath its young. Your line was spread the wings. Who did you protect gently? Today, the last portion of the Torah begins. Day five hundred thirty-two.

Think about last words. At a hospital bedside, at an airport gate, at the end of a long phone call with someone far away. Some last words are instructions: take care of your mother. Some are worries. Some are apologies. The ones people remember for decades are usually something else. The Torah's final portion opens with Moses' last words to the people. He has warned them, taught them, argued with them and sung to them. Now he does one more thing.
screen: `AT THE BEDSIDE, AT THE GATE.` → `INSTRUCTIONS, WORRIES, APOLOGIES.` → `ONE MORE THING.`

segments.voice: "And this is the blessing, wherewith Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death." In Hebrew, v'zot haberachah: and this is the blessing. It's the one portion never read on an ordinary Shabbat. It's read on Simchat Torah, the day the yearly cycle ends and begins again. Notice the title Moses is given here: the man of God. This verse is the first place the Torah calls him that. After a lifetime of leading, his final role is to bless. Then he goes tribe by tribe, the way his ancestor Jacob blessed his sons at the end of Genesis. Each tribe receives something different. For Judah, that its voice be heard. For Levi, the work of teaching. For Zebulun, the riches of the sea. For Asher, a foot dipped in olive oil. Not one blessing copied twelve times. Each one fits. Rashi stops at the words before his death and reads them as close to his death. If not now, when? There's no more time to wait. Moses has been angry with these people, disappointed by them, worn out by them. He doesn't end with any of that. He ends with a blessing for each one, by name. This week walked from the hidden face to here. Hidden, not gone. Heaven and earth listen. Drop as the rain. The rock. Ask your elders. Spread the wings. And now: end with a blessing.
screen: `V'ZOT HABERACHAH.` · `MOSES, THE MAN OF GOD.` · `EACH TRIBE ITS OWN BLESSING.` · `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?` · then, large: `END WITH A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end your day by blessing someone. Settle, and breathe. Think ahead to tonight, the last part of your day. Who will you see, or call, or think of? Many Jewish parents bless their children on Friday night with the old priestly words: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee." If you pray, you can use those words for someone tonight. If you don't, a specific wish will do, shaped to them, the way Moses shaped each tribe's. Choose the person now. The bell holds the time.
V'Zot HaBerachah. And this is the blessing. The last portion of the Torah, and Moses' last words.
Your line: end with a blessing. Tonight, before you sleep, bless one person, aloud or in your heart, with words that fit them. Day five hundred thirty-two.
